note: Hand-curated landmarks beyond the Solar System. ra/dec in degrees (J2000). Distance is given once: ly (light-years, Milky Way and its satellites), mly (million light-years, nearby universe) or z (redshift; the site computes light-travel time and present-day distance from it with Planck 2018 ΛCDM). approx marks positions or distances known only roughly. sig = spin period in milliseconds for pulsars. mass = solar masses for black holes. size = diameter in the same unit as the distance (ly, or million ly when mly or z is given).

items.note: The Sun sits inside a cavity about 1,000 light-years across, blown out by a series of supernovae that began some 14 million years ago. Nearly all the star-forming clouds near us lie on its surface.
The nearest open cluster, the V-shaped face of Taurus. Eddington's 1919 eclipse expedition measured starlight bending past the Sun against this cluster.
About a thousand stars only 100 million years old, still wrapped in a dust cloud they happen to be drifting through. Their distance was argued over for decades until Gaia settled it.
A nearby pulsar almost silent in radio, found by its gamma rays. The supernova that made it may have helped carve the Local Bubble.
The nearest millisecond pulsar, spinning 174 times a second. Its ticks are stable enough to use in the search for gravitational waves from merging supermassive black holes.
One of the nearest planetary nebulae: the outer layers of a Sun-like star, thrown off and lit by the white dwarf left behind. This is roughly what the Sun will do in five billion years.
The spinning core of a star that exploded about 11,000 years ago. It turns 11 times a second and is the brightest steady source of gamma rays in the sky.
The first pulsar, found by Jocelyn Bell in 1967 as a quarter-inch of scruff on a chart recorder. Its pulses arrive every 1.3373 seconds.
The nearest large stellar nursery, visible to the naked eye as the middle star of Orion's sword. Hubble found discs of planet-forming dust around hundreds of its young stars.
A dark pillar of dust silhouetted against glowing hydrogen. The red background is the hydrogen-alpha line this site takes its accent colour from.
The first planets found outside the Solar System orbit this dead star. They were detected in 1992 because they tug the pulsar and shift the arrival times of its pulses.
The shock wave of a supernova that went off 10,000 to 20,000 years ago, still sweeping up gas. The red filaments are hydrogen and the blue-green are oxygen.

A planetary nebula with eleven concentric shells, each a pulse of mass thrown off about every 1,500 years. In 1864 it was the first nebula examined with a spectroscope, which showed it was gas and not stars.
The remains of the supernova seen in 1054. It spins about 30 times a second and powers the whole Crab Nebula as it slows down.
The first object widely accepted to be a black hole, about 21 solar masses, stripping gas from a blue supergiant. Stephen Hawking bet against it and conceded in 1990.
A pair of stars, the larger over 100 solar masses, that erupted in the 1840s and briefly became the second-brightest star in the sky. It survived, and will end as a supernova.
Four times the size of the Orion Nebula. One of Webb's first images showed the Cosmic Cliffs at its edge.
The youngest known supernova remnant in the Milky Way; its light arrived around 1680 and almost nobody noticed. Outside the Solar System it is the brightest radio source in the sky.
A ball of about a million stars, 12 billion years old. It holds more than 40 millisecond pulsars.
The largest globular cluster of the Milky Way, probably the stripped core of a galaxy it swallowed. Fast stars near its centre point to a black hole of at least 8,200 solar masses.
Two neutron stars orbiting every 7.75 hours. Their orbit shrinks by 76 microseconds a year, exactly as predicted if they radiate gravitational waves: the first evidence that such waves exist.

The black hole at the centre of the Milky Way: 4.3 million solar masses inside a region smaller than Mercury's orbit. Light takes about 85 seconds to cross its event horizon. Zoom in until the black disc appears and watch what it does to the stars behind it.
A magnetar that in April 2020 produced a millisecond radio burst bright enough to be seen from another galaxy. It tied fast radio bursts to magnetars for the first time.
A small galaxy on the far side of the Milky Way's centre, being pulled apart into streams of stars that wrap around the whole sky.
The Milky Way's largest satellite, visible to the naked eye from the southern hemisphere. It probably arrived only in the last couple of billion years and is on its first pass.
The nearest supernova since the telescope was invented, seen on 24 February 1987. About two dozen of its neutrinos were caught on Earth roughly three hours before the light arrived.
Henrietta Leavitt found the period–luminosity law of Cepheid variables in photographs of this galaxy. That law became the first rung of the extragalactic distance ladder.
A faint satellite galaxy that is almost entirely dark matter: its stars move far too fast for the light it gives off.
A dwarf spheroidal galaxy with six globular clusters of its own.
One of the most distant satellites of the Milky Way, hidden in the glare of Regulus. Its motion is used to weigh the whole Milky Way.
A giant elliptical galaxy that would be one of the brightest in the sky if the dust of the Milky Way were not in front of it. It was found in 1967, in infrared.
The first black hole ever imaged, in April 2019: 6.5 billion solar masses at the heart of the galaxy M87. Its shadow is wider than the whole Solar System, and it drives a jet 5,000 light-years long.
The nearest rich cluster, 1,300 to 2,000 galaxies, with M87 at its heart. The Local Group is falling toward it.
The second-richest cluster within 100 million light-years, compact and dominated by the giant elliptical NGC 1399.
A nearly empty region that begins at the edge of the Local Group. Its emptiness pushes us away at about 260 km/s.
The gravitational centre of Laniakea, toward which our whole region flows. It lies behind the plane of the Milky Way, which is why it took until the 1980s to find and the 1990s to map.
The supercluster that contains the Milky Way, defined in 2014 not by where galaxies are but by which way they flow. About 100,000 galaxies over 520 million light-years.
Sound waves from its central black hole ripple through the cluster gas. The note is a B-flat 57 octaves below middle C.
A long chain of clusters on the far side of the Local Void, one of the largest structures in the nearby universe.
More than a thousand galaxies. In 1933 Fritz Zwicky found they move too fast to be held by the matter he could see, and named the remainder dark matter.
The first great wall, found in 1989: a sheet of galaxies 500 million light-years long running through the Coma Cluster. It showed that galaxies lie on the walls of enormous bubbles.
Holds the scar of the most energetic explosion known: an outburst from its central black hole that hollowed out a cavity fifteen Milky Ways across.
A young, irregular cluster rich in spirals, still assembling from smaller groups.
The most massive concentration of galaxies in the nearby universe. Laniakea as a whole is drifting toward it.

A sphere 330 million light-years across with about 60 known galaxies inside, where thousands would be expected. If the Milky Way sat at its centre, other galaxies would not have been discovered until the 1960s.
One of the brightest radio sources in the sky. Twin jets from its black hole end in lobes 500,000 light-years apart.
A filament of galaxies 1.37 billion light-years long, found in 2003. Whether it is one bound structure or a chance alignment is still debated.
Its central galaxy, IC 1101, is among the largest known, with a faint halo of stars reaching millions of light-years from its centre.
The brightest gamma-ray burst ever recorded, on 9 October 2022. Its flash disturbed Earth's upper atmosphere from 1.9 billion light-years away.
The first quasar identified. In 1963 Maarten Schmidt realised its strange spectral lines were ordinary hydrogen shifted by 16%, which meant something star-like was outshining whole galaxies.
One of the most powerful gravitational lenses known. Its mass smears background galaxies into more than a hundred arcs.
The first fast radio burst seen to repeat, which ruled out a one-off explosion as its cause. It was traced to a dwarf galaxy three billion light-years away.

Two clusters that passed through each other. The hot gas collided and stayed in the middle while the mass, mapped by lensing, sailed on: the most direct evidence that dark matter is a substance and not a quirk of gravity.
Flares roughly every 12 years, as would happen if a second black hole were punching through the disc of an 18-billion-solar-mass one.
The cluster in Webb's first deep field, released on 11 July 2022. The patch of sky is the size of a grain of sand held at arm's length.
A complex of superclusters about a billion light-years across, reported in 2016.
The most massive known cluster at its distance: two clusters colliding at several million kilometres an hour when the universe was half its present age.

A clustering of gamma-ray bursts reported in 2013 that would mark a structure 10 billion light-years long, larger than standard cosmology comfortably allows. Later analyses disagree on whether it is real.
A quasar powered by one of the most massive black holes measured, around 40 billion Suns. Its event horizon is more than 25 times wider than Neptune's orbit.
Surrounded by the largest reservoir of water vapour known: about 140 trillion times the water in Earth's oceans, already there 12 billion years ago.
The most luminous quasar known, announced in 2024. Its black hole swallows about a Sun's worth of matter every day.
The most distant single star ever seen, visible only because a galaxy cluster in front of it magnifies its light thousands of times.
A black hole of 800 million solar masses that already existed 690 million years after the Big Bang. How anything grew that large that fast is an open problem.
One of the most distant quasars known: 1.6 billion solar masses when the universe was 670 million years old.
The death of a star 630 million years after the Big Bang, seen on 23 April 2009. For a while it was the most distant object of any kind ever observed.
Found by Hubble in 2016 and for six years the most distant galaxy known. Webb later showed it is surprisingly bright and rich in nitrogen for something so young.
Confirmed by Webb's spectrograph in 2022 at a time 320 million years after the Big Bang.
Bright, 1,600 light-years across and already containing oxygen less than 300 million years after the Big Bang. Galaxies this mature this early were not expected.
Reported in 2025 as the most distant galaxy with a measured spectrum: its light left about 280 million years after the Big Bang.

Light leaving a galaxy beyond this distance today will never reach us, however long we wait, because the space in between expands faster than the light can cross it. We still see those galaxies only because their old light was already on its way.

Everything beyond this distance is receding from us faster than light. That breaks no law: nothing is moving through space faster than light; the space in between is growing. Most of the galaxies Webb photographs lie outside it.
No telescope has seen this far yet. Somewhere around here the first stars lit up in a universe that had been dark since the afterglow of the Big Bang faded.

The oldest light there is, released when the universe was about 380,000 years old and cool enough to become transparent. Every direction you look ends at this wall. The mottled pattern drawn here is illustrative; the real one varies by one part in 100,000.

The present-day distance to the most distant matter whose light could ever have reached us: about 46 billion light-years in every direction, even though the universe is only 13.8 billion years old, because space kept expanding while the light was in transit.
